# Global Markets: Same Engine, New Leaders


October 1, 2026


[Nick Niziolek](https://www.calamos.com/about/investment-organization/nick-niziolek/) , CFA,[Dennis Cogan](https://www.calamos.com/about/portfolio-management/dennis-cogan/) , CFA,[Paul Ryndak](https://www.calamos.com/about/portfolio-management/paul-ryndak/) , CFA, and[Kyle Ruge](https://www.calamos.com/about/portfolio-management/kyle-ruge/) , CFA


[Last quarter](https://www.calamos.com/blogs/voices/global-markets-fundamentals-have-the-floor/) , we wrote that fundamentals had the floor: markets were rewarding earnings growth, thematic tailwinds were strong, and the potential for rapid shifts in macro conditions called for flexibility and balance. The third quarter put that view to the test, but our outlook remains positive. We continue to believe the AI buildout is one of the most powerful growth engines in the global economy and that it remains in its early stages. At the same time, the opportunity set within AI is evolving quickly, macro crosswinds have intensified, and the case for balance is stronger than it was three months ago.


After a strong first half of the year, AI leadership rotated during the quarter. Many semiconductor, hardware, and power-related stocks that had led the rally pulled back, while the largest AI spenders and software companies took the lead. Broader global equity markets had modestly positive returns. We view this as a digestion of an exceptionally strong run, not a turn in the fundamentals behind it. During the quarter, several of the largest cloud providers ramped up their spending plans again, with some signaling that capacity constraints could persist into 2027. Still, even earnings-driven markets can move faster than earnings in the short run, and corrections tend to land hardest on those equities that performed the best leading into the correction.


Our confidence that we are in the earlier stages of this multiyear buildout only increased during the quarter. Demand is broadening beyond the largest US platforms to AI labs, specialized cloud providers, governments investing in sovereign capacity, and enterprises moving from pilots to production. Spending is gradually shifting from training models to running them at scale, which should require more compute, memory, networking, and power over time. Physical constraints in power generation, grid connections, advanced packaging, and memory capacity may slow the buildout, but they will likely take years to resolve, which extends the runway and creates new opportunities along the way.


How we are positioned within this theme will keep evolving. Early leadership went to the most direct suppliers of computing power, but as the buildout matured, bottlenecks migrated to memory, components, packaging, and power, with market leadership following suit. Over time, we expect the opportunity to shift toward companies that use AI to grow revenue and margins, as the market becomes more discerning about the returns on this spending. We have begun rotating some of our exposure toward companies showing a positive inflection from AI-related investments, and we expect to continue rotating within and across themes as the opportunity set evolves. Near term, sentiment around AI infrastructure could remain volatile, with markets quick to reward good news and just as quick to punish disappointments.


The macro backdrop is bifurcated. AI spending continues to power growth, while renewed hostilities involving Iran have kept energy prices elevated and complicated an already elevated inflation picture. A tightening cycle is underway across much of the world, and long-dated sovereign yields have broken out to multi-decade highs, reflecting both this dynamic and the broader demand for growth capital. Credit spreads have been contained but bear close watching, as more AI spending is financed with debt.


Rising rates are landing hardest on the lower leg of the so-called K-shaped economy, including housing, lower- and middle-income consumers, and some small businesses outside AI—areas that already looked soft. The question is whether modest tightening can cool inflation without toppling those consumers and small businesses, and possibly the AI-driven economy, too. Our base case is a mid-cycle slowdown that still supports reasonable equity returns.


Against this backdrop, balance matters. Other important themes include defense and industrial rearmament, grid buildout, and precision health and life sciences. We also hold adjacent beneficiaries of AI spending and fiscal expansion, including select financials and industrials, where we see opportunities that could prove durable for several more years. More defensive businesses with less cyclical cash flows should provide stability if conditions turn more turbulent.


## Conclusion


We are optimistic about global equities and believe the AI buildout will be a central driver of earnings growth for years to come. However, we expect third-quarter volatility to persist, and we’re watching several signposts: the situation in the Middle East and energy prices; central bank policy and financial conditions; the pace of AI capital spending and the related political and regulatory backdrop; and the US elections in November.


We are confident that the defining principles of our approach—including our active management of risk/reward, thematic and fundamental research, valuation discipline, and commitment to respecting the wisdom of the markets—will serve the portfolios well.
